newsitem.title: CANADA: Shell Canada knows of no sale in works.
newsitem.headline: Shell Canada knows of no sale in works.

text.p: Shell Canada Ltd's C$635 million sale of its chemicals business is aimed at streamlining its operations, and is not due to any impending sale by its 78-percent owner, Royal Dutch/Shell Group, a Shell Canada executive said on Tuesday.
"To the best of our knowledge, the shareholder has no intention of selling any further interest in the other parts of our business," said Shell Canada vice-president Ron Blakely.
"You have to distinguish between this chemical business and it being a global business and the rest of our business, (which) is essentially North American-focused."
Shell Canada, Canada's second-largest integrated oil company by 1995 revenues, produces oil, gas and sulphur and is a major refiner and gasoline marketer.

Blakely said the company's chemicals division, which includes a major styrene plant at Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was set to contribute C$40 million to the company's earnings in 1996, well below the C$221 million earned last year.
Much of the drop was due to styrene prices, which have fallen to about US$0.23 per pound on the U.S. Gulf Coast from US$0.46 in the first quarter of 1995, he said.
Shell Canada said Tuesday it would sell its chemicals division to a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
The sale includes Shell Canada's 450,000 metric ton per year styrene plant in Fort Saskatchewan and isopropyl alcohol facilties in Sarnia, Ontario, as well as all related marketing activities.
To be successful in today's petrochemicals business, companies require size and worldwide scope, Blakely said.
To bne successful

"You have to have a global infrastructure, you've got to have plants in parts of the world that serve that global market and in Shell Canada's case we have one plant, one commodity chemical. It really is over the long run unsustainable," Blakely said.
Analysts on Tuesday said the division was being sold to Shell International at an extremely favorable price to Shell Canada.
"The got a hell of a price for it -- I never would have thought they would have gotten this kind of dollars," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp.
Molyneaux said he had estimated the value of the deal to be nearly C$4 per share on an after-tax basis, about C$1 per share higher than his estimated net asset value.
He said he was expecting earnings per share from Shell Canada's chemicals division of C$0.43 and cash flow per share of C$0.53. "So they got almost 11 times this year's cash flow," he said.
Blakely said he "would not take issue" with analyst views that Shell Canada would have about C$800 million in cash and marketable securities after the sale, expected at year-end.

The war chest could be used for various initiatives, such as a share buyback, asset acquisitions or spending on Shell's major projects, which currently include the Sable Island offshore natural gas project and a possible full-scale oil sands project, said Molyneaux.
Analysts said they could not get a reading from Tuesday's deal whether Royal/Dutch Shell was setting Shell Canada up for a sale. The sale rumors have circulated for several years.
Several agreed, however, that it was difficult to envision Canada being one of a few nations in the world without a large Shell presence.
-- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
